question: Which of the following statement is NOT true for the magnetic field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid?

options.text: Ellipsoidal and intersects with each other
Along the axis and parallel to each other
The same at all points inside the solenoid

solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Magnetic field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid are **uniform** and **parallel to each other** along the axis of the solenoid.
 
• The field inside the solenoid is **the same at all points** and is considered to be uniform in strength.
 
• The field lines do not intersect each other; they run **parallel** to the axis and are evenly spaced, indicating a uniform field.
 
• The statement that the field lines are "ellipsoidal and intersect with each other" is incorrect, as magnetic field lines never cross each other.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Current-Carrying Solenoid:**

 
 
• A solenoid is a coil of wire designed to create a magnetic field when an electric current passes through it.
 
• When current flows through the solenoid, it generates a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet, with distinct north and south poles.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic Field Lines:**
 
 
• Magnetic field lines are a visual representation of the magnetic field, showing the direction and strength of the field.
 
• They always form closed loops, emerging from the north pole and entering the south pole of a magnet.
 
 
 
• **Properties of Magnetic Field Lines:**
 
 
• Magnetic field lines never intersect; if they did, it would imply multiple directions for the magnetic field at a single point, which is impossible.
 
 
• **Applications of Solenoids:**
 
 
• Solenoids are used in various applications including electromagnets, inductors, valves, and as components in electromechanical devices such as relays.
 
• They are also used in scientific experiments and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines to create controlled magnetic fields.
